utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar, good morning to you. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Oric, good morning to you. Can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, distinguished gentlemen. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. Good morning also to the Defence team. I'm here together with co-counsel Ms. Joanne Richardson, and our case manager Ms. Djurdja Mirkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you and your team. Ms. Mirkovic, welcome back. We haven't seen you for some time. Appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Vasvija Vidovic, together with Mr. John Jones, appearing on behalf of Mr. Naser Oric. Joining us are our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, as well as our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I thank you, Madam Vidovic, and good morning to you and your team. Before we start with the new witness, are there any preliminaries? Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just three brief preliminaries. The first is that we'll file our reply on the issue of authentication tomorrow. I hope that will be deemed in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perfect, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. The second is that we received from the Prosecution late last night, yesterday evening, a list of exhibits to be used with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have the same problem that we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The thing is I don't want to jump the gun because the Prosecution might not necessarily intend to be using all of these exhibits with this witness, but I do note that there are about 30 exhibits. Most of them have got nothing to do with this witness. And to anticipate -- I see my learned friend is on her feet, but perhaps I can finish making my submission first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, finish. Go ahead, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. The point is to anticipate if what the Prosecution intends to do is elicit evidence from this witness that he was in prison with such and such a person that perhaps they were from this village, that they had this wife, and then to present the document and say, "Is this what is contained in this document," then in my submission that would be a large waste of time because the Prosecution can elicit that evidence and then subsequently can make the argument that the evidence in the -- that the information in the document is correct. And indeed, I adopted that approach with Ms. Filipovic, you may recall, when looking at the Sokolac collection. I started embarking on points about the documents with her, and they aren't documents for her. In my submission many of these issues are not going to be issues which this witness can help us with at all. He's not the author of the document, he can't authenticate the document, the documents are not about him. It's really firstly, just to anticipate that, and anticipate our submission that would be a fruitless exercise. And then the third issue is simply just to say with this witness, we would appreciate full -- wish the Prosecution would not lead when it comes to the actual detention, with circumstances of detention, and particularly not suggest names to the witness. Really, I think it's only fair with this witness that he provide any names, and that no names be suggested to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to the first submission by Mr. Jones, proofing continued -- started on Saturday, ended on Sunday, and as such we were not able to determine, until we had spoken with the witness, exactly what exhibits we would have introduced -- we would seek to introduce with him. Secondly, I submit with respect to the documents at hand, that the Prosecution be permitted to put any and all relevant information that we deem relevant to the witness. And certainly if these documents are deemed irrelevant at the time, I'm sure the Bench can make a decision about that. In fact, we should at least wait until these documents are presented to the witness. He can comment on them, as need be. And I submit to Your Honour that the documents are, in fact, relevant. They do go to what he observed personally during his detention. And as such, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll see. We'll come to that when we come to that when we need to use these documents but experience teaches that sometimes of them become useful, some of them are rendered redundant. Anyway, we'll pursue that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the last one, I think you know what the rules are. The position that will be taken is that if, at any time, in matters relight to the detention of this person, the Defence feels that the Prosecution is leading, you raise an objection and it will be decided accordingly. If you don't raise objections, the Chamber will adopt the system practised that it has adopted so far. We'll will look the other way, in other words, because that's the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. And in relation to that, and again not to anticipate points about the documents, but if the witness were presented documents before he deals with certain issues, we would see that as a form of leading because he's having information suggested to him. Again, it's a matter which we'll see in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll come to that then. And, if possible, the last thing I wanted to say is this: That our secretaries, our respective secretaries, got the list this morning with the result that -- you know, I mean it's not practical at all. We got the list. We don't know what these documents are. We end up with binders and folders and whatever. It's not exactly what we would prefer --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand. And again, I just want to reiterate, the witness, we were unable to send this list out until we had spoken with the witness. But with respect to the timing of those documents and when they will be used, I anticipate using those documents at the very end of the direct examination. So I suspect that quite possibly I may not get to them tomorrow, if I go over today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And how much time do you anticipate you will need for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I anticipate that -- well, this witness has a lot of information to present to this Court, a lot of evidence, and I anticipate finishing tomorrow morning, probably an hour into the morning session, at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think probably around three hours, then, in that case, if the Prosecution will be four and a half hours with this witness. I was thinking more like two, two and a half hours. But in light of what Ms. Richardson said, it seems that quite a lot will come to light.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It also depends on what he says, on what he testifies. Let's start. Any further matters you would like to discuss? None? Let's see the witness. You can lead in the initial period, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will be speaking in English, and you should be receiving interpretation of what I am saying in your own language. I want to make sure, first and foremost, before I proceed, that what I am saying in English is being interpreted in your own language, and that you are receiving it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome once more. Welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are going to give evidence, a case that has been ongoing against Naser Oric. Our Rules require that before you start testifying, you make a solemn declaration equivalent to an oath, in a sense that in the course of your testimony, you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text of this solemn declaration is contained in a piece of paper that Madam Usher is going to hand to you now. Please take that document in your hand, read out the text aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with this Tribunal that you will be testifying the truth. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please take a seat. Have you ever given evidence in a court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not here, or in my own country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I need to explain to you very briefly what is going to happen. You have been summoned here by the Prosecution, but the moment you sit where you're sitting now, you become a witness of this Tribunal. The procedure that will be followed is the Prosecution will go first. They will spend about three to four hours firing questions at you which you will need to answer to the best of your ability. And if you can, if you are in a position to answer those questions, then you need to answer those questions truthfully and as fully as possible. When Ms. Richardson is finished with her series of questions, then Mr. Jones, who is one of the lawyers representing Mr. Oric, will begin his cross-examination, which will consist of about another three hours of questions which you also need to answer to the best of your ability. And if you are in a position to answer those questions, then obviously you need to answer them as truthfully and as fully as when you answered the questions of the Prosecution. In other words, you do not have the right to distinguish between the Prosecution and the Defence. You don't belong either to the Prosecution or to the Defence, you belong to the Tribunal. And your responsibility in terms of the oath that you have just taken is to answer all the questions truthfully and fully. Have I made myself clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Clear enough, thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. If at any time, Mr. Ivanovic, you need a break, you feel tired -- I know that you'll be testifying about events that are not easy to testify about. If at any time you feel uncomfortable, you feel tired, you need a break, please attract -- do draw my attention, and I'm sure that we will be able to, and we'll be able to help you. Incidentally, I am presiding over this trial. My name is Carmel Agius, and I come from Malta. To my right I have Judge Hans Hendrik Brydensholt from Denmark, and to my left Judge Albin Eser from Germany. So, welcome. Ms. Richardson, you can start with her direct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Ms. Richardson:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning. Please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Ilija Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And please confirm the following information with a verbal yes: You were born the 1st of February, 1961; you are married; you are a Serb; and you received training as a plumber and currently work as a plumber privately.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were born in the village of Cosici, which is in Srebrenica municipality, and this is approximately 7 kilometres from Skelani; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You presently live in Bajina Basta, which is just across the bridge from the Drina River, from Skelani. And you resided in Bajina Basta in 1992, but you frequently returned to the village where your parents lived. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in 1992 -- well, I should first ask: The village of Cosici is a Serb village, and it's approximately 13 houses, and the main source of income is agriculture.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: That's correct. Everything you've just stated is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in 1992, you were in the village of Cosici, and you were part of a village guard.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The village guard had uniforms and some weapons; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you briefly state how many men were in the village guard, and what types of weapons you used.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: We were about 25 in the village, 25 men who stood guard around the village. The village was under threat by the Muslim forces, so we had to watch over our homes. It was as simple as that, really. We had different kinds of weapons. Some had hunting rifles; some had PAP rifles; some had automatic rifles. That was about all that we had. Later on we were given a mortar that was also positioned inside the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did there come a time that you also, the village guard also placed land mines in and around the village?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes. We laid mines at the point where the nearest village to us, Bozici, had been set alight. We were already quite frightened, so we laid mines along a road where we believed the enemy might come from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you receive -- did the village guard receive training from the Serb military or the Serb army?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: No. No, nothing like that. Never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to bring your attention next to January 16th of 1993. Do you recall that day?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes, I recall it only too well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what happened on that day? Did there come a time -- I'll rephrase that question. Could you tell us what happened at what time you woke up that day?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: On that day, if you bear in mind that there were about 25 men guarding the village, half of those were standing guard and half were asleep, they were resting. At that point in time, I happened to be in my mother's house. I was asleep. Suddenly, at a quarter to six, you could hear mine explosions. One of my relatives said, "I'm going to get up now. I can hear sounds of some sort of a weapon firing." We started out; however, shooting began. At that moment, one of my relatives said, "We are under attack."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who were you under attack -- who were -- who did you believe was attacking the village, and could you see where the attack was coming from?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: The attack came from all sides. We were entirely surrounded, the village was, I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what, if anything, did you do at that point?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: At that point we deployed ourselves in order to be able to defend ourselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you, in fact, defend the village?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, could you see the actual people that were attacking you?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes. At first -- well, first of all, I must say this was going on at the crack of dawn. The Muslim forces were attacking us and penetrating into the village, and they were burning houses as they were going along. The greatest damage was inflicted on us by snipers from across the river, from the neighbouring village. At one point in time I saw a long column of Muslims, men, women and children, moving from Colakovici, in our direction. Livestock, too, horses probably that they were using for looting and for taking away whatever they looted in a particular village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which village did you see these Muslim individuals taking -- looting? Could you tell which village this was actually occurring in? Was this your village or another village?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Specifically in relation to my village, that's all I can tell you, what I saw. But I heard from other people that more or less the same thing was being done in all the other villages that were first looted and then burned down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you were able to visibly see who the snipers were or who was doing the shooting?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: No. My village is in a cold place, and we were locked in ice. They were sniping at us from across the river, and their view of us was perfectly clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned it was in a cold place. Could you tell us what the weather conditions were that day? Was there snow on the ground?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the area of my village and Gradina, which is where I was captured, there was snow on the ground, and the rest was further to the east, across the river and towards the village of Bozici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as the village guards attempted to defend the village, what did the civilian villagers do at that point?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: The moment we noticed that this was an attack, we asked all the civilians to withdraw towards Maltasi, across Skelani and on towards Bajina Basta. That was at about 6.00 a.m., because the attack first began at a quarter to six. Once we tried to get the civilians evacuated, once we got the civilians evacuated, we remained and tried to put up some resistance, believing that we could preserve the village; however, we failed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson, Judge Eser would like to put a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I would have a question to the Prosecution. Could you provide us with a map so that it would be easier for us to follow the location of the different places, and from there, just as that happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, indeed I can. I do have a copy -- I do have a map. However, we were not able to make copies -- because I hadn't decided whether or not I would use it. But I can put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Put it on the ELMO, at least, so that the public can follow better and we can follow better, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, could you take a look at the map that's on the ELMO. And if you look at that map closely, could you point to where your village is located on the map. And if it's not on the map, please just, with a pen, draw where your village would have been -- would have been located on that map.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness seems to be pointing somewhere. Perhaps we could ...

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Could you tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could we zoom --

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I can't find the village of Cosici marked here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't be surprised. We're talking of a small hamlet of 13 houses, I would be very surprised to find it on a map, unless it is one of those really military survey maps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Maybe we can do this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you, Mr. Ivanovic, could you circle Bajina Basta on that map, or Skelani, if you can. And from there, possibly point to where your village would have been located on that map, approximately.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that where your village would have been located on this map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That would be Cosici?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Cosici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Cosici, yes. So --

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I do know that it is located between Bozici and Kolari or Arapovici. But I can't really, perhaps, draw it up precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't worry about it. The important thing is that we have an idea. Could I ask you to put your initials next to that small circle that you put, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is Cosici on a hill or in a valley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A valley, next to the river.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ivanovic, where were -- I asked you before, but I'm not sure you answered. Where were the civilians during the attack? Were they trying to flee the village?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: The civilians were in their homes, and following this attack, starting at a quarter to six when we realised that there was an attack going on, they went out of their houses and we told them to go towards Maltasi and then on towards Bajina Basta, because we thought this was the only passable route to Bajina Basta.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anyone killed during the attack, anyone from your village?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes. Out of the 25 of us, 12 were killed. Twelve of the men and a woman who was taken out of the village and probably killed somewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that there were snipers. Could you tell us where the snipers were located? Could you tell the direction they were shooting from?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: From the direction of Bozici, from across the river, from the direction of Bozici, probably from some barns and other shelters. We were unable to spot them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a point that you were -- yourself and the other village guards were unable to continue defending the village from attack?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes. We came under attack from all directions, from weapons of different calibre, but this was all to no avail. We were soon surrounded. And at one point, when we noticed that we were unable to defend the village, we decided to pull out. There were people who were killed by snipers. And in this attempt to withdraw, there was an uncle of mine who was shot by a sniper. I tried to grab him with my hand. He just yelled, "Let go." So the moment I tried to grab him, luckily for me, it was at this particular point that another shot was fired from a sniper, and as I leant forward to grab my uncle, the shot missed me. He, however, died a minute later. He was shot in the neck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, before we move on to what happened after your uncle was killed, you mentioned that you could see Muslim men and women looting. Could you tell us if these individuals were in civilian clothing, or were they wearing any kind of uniform that you could see as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: He mentioned children as well, and that should be --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they wearing civilian clothing or --

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: There was this enormous column stretching out for perhaps a kilometre from the direction of Colakovici. And I've told you that these were mostly looters who would barge into villages, loot, and then torch everything. They were wearing different clothes, depending on what their circumstances were. And it was difficult for me to take all this in, to pay attention to this. But I know that they did wear different types of clothes. As they were moving from Colakovici towards Cosici, you could hear this enormous noise, the banging and the singing and the yelling, probably aimed at intimidating us who were defending our village and homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were any of these people that you observed looting, including the children, was anyone in uniform? Could you tell from where you were?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: The only thing that I could notice was that they were wearing their army's uniforms, those multicoloured ones. And they had bands on their arms and on their heads, red and blue ones. I noticed the red and blue bands later on as well when I was captured. But at the time in Cosici, I noticed the red bands only.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mentioned that the houses were being burned. Could you tell who was actually burning the houses from where you were at that point?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Of course I could see that, because it was the soldiers who barged into the village who set everything ablaze. It was the Muslims. And I could not really think of anyone else who would be there at that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After your uncle was killed, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: It was not my uncle, actually, it was my cousin, my uncle's son.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And his name?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Zeljko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after --

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Zeljko Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after he was killed, what happened next?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: At that point the shooting continued. Many of the men were killed, and we continued with the evacuation. I continued withdrawing in the direction of the village of Maltasi. At one point when I was crawling along the ice, one of my relatives, Mile, who had managed to pull out earlier on, knowing that his son had been killed, he was returning to the village. I told him, "Where do you think you're going? Almost everybody has been killed." So we continued crawling in the direction of Maltasi, pulling out, and it was just by happenstance that I managed to get out of the village alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you could look at the map on the ELMO, it may be helpful to the Trial Chamber. Could you point to the direction you were crawling in from your village? Where were you going? If you're unable to find it, that's fine, we can continue.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I can't locate Maltasi on this map, and that would help me get my bearings here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you look at Skelani, if you look -- do you see Bajina Basta? Bajina Basta?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Now, at 10.00, there is Skelani.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And at 11.00, there is Malta.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Indicates]. I have found Maltasi, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We do have copies of the map, if we can have the usher's assistance in handing them out at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It would be a big surprise if I didn't manage to find my own place.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And at this stage I believe we would need a Prosecution's exhibit number for this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall we give it a number? This would be P?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it would be P472.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: P472. Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this time were you with anyone, as you were trying to crawl out of your village?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes. I was with Mile Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did anything happen as you -- were you armed? Did you have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes, I did have a weapon. And my relative, Mijo, did as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any other type of -- did you have a grenade with you as well?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after you were crawling, you were crawling along for some time?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes. I was crawling for a kilometre and a half, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during that point in time, were you able to see anyone, namely, any of the attackers, or see anyone else in that area?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes. As I was pulling out, above the village of Pavkovici, in the direction of Maltaska Gradina, I could see them crossing over from the village of Pavkovici to Cosici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say "them," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I was referring to the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how were they dressed? Could you tell what -- were they wearing uniforms, so it's clear to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: As far as I could discern, some of them were in uniforms and -- that is, they all had different types of uniforms. Some were in camouflage uniforms; some were in other types of uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did there come a point in time where you were no longer crawling and you came to a stop?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes. I stopped crawling as I came across a brook, and from there I started pulling out towards what we call Maltaska Gradina. I turned around and saw that everything was ablaze, I mean the village that I was in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: After that, when I reached Maltaska Gradina, unaware that this place had also come under attack, I knew that in this particular village there were also people standing guard, just as we had in the village of Cosici. As I crossed this top of the hill, there was a valley that I hid in. Later on I was trying to find somebody from Maltasi, to draw their attention to me so that they wouldn't shoot at me. However, as I stood up, while I was in this valley, there was this brook running across the valley and across from there I saw a large group of Muslims, women as well, armed. They were dressed in different clothes. The girls, depending on what they had, some would have a camouflage coat, perhaps, and then a pair of jeans and boots and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "girls," approximately what ages were these girls?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: They were all very young. I never saw an elderly person among them in the army. The elderly ones were looters; they would take away whatever they could carry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said -- let me just clarify this point again. When you say "girls," you're not referring to children, are you referring to young women or in their early twenties or late teens?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I don't see why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- when she says "girls" he should be referring to children. That's a strange -- yes, well Ms. Richardson has just said, "When you say 'girls' you're not referring to children. Well, I don't see where that comes from. Why should he not be referring to children when he says "girls." Perhaps she -- she should just ask the ages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson, I think Mr. Jones is -- I mean, I don't -- I don't refer to you as a girl. I mean I refer to you as a woman.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that's what I'm trying to get out of the witness, the exact ages so that we're clear it's not children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go straight to the point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the approximate ages of girls you described in uniforms or partial uniforms?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: They were from 17 to 20 years of age. Perhaps some of them were younger. I can't really say. But if I meant to say that they were children, I would have said that. And when I say a girl, I mean a young woman, then you could probably deduce what sort of age they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were they also carrying weapons?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes, they were. All of them had weapons of much better quality than we did. All of them were automatic weapons. Let me explain to you. When my cousin was killed, he was wearing a semi-automatic rifle, and as they killed him, they just left the rifle standing there, they refused to take it with them. Then you can imagine what sort of weaponry they had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you able to see anything else from that point, or did anything happen after you were able to get a vision of these individuals?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: It was only after I was captured by them that I could see some more. I was taken to this meadow where there were several captured women and a boy, a child.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Before we get to your capture, could you tell us about how -- tell us about the circumstances surrounding your capture. How was it that you were captured after you were crawling along and you came to a stop?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: As my cousin and I were pulling out, we were talking about how we should make sure not to fall into their hands, that it was better for us to be killed than be captured by them. In this small valley where we were, my cousin laid down prone, having a grenade beneath his stomach, and I lay on my back. But my relative, he knew that his son had been killed, so he was just there, resigned. And without telling me anything, the grenade was activated and threw him all over to this bank of this brook. And I was, myself, wounded by this grenade; I had wounds in my face and hands. At that point we heard, "Surrender, Chetniks. We can see you." This panic ensued. I barely managed to get out of this pool of water. As I managed to reach this hillock, they kicked me in my face. Some of them hit me with their rifle butt. They were swearing at me. And then there was this sudden silence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, I just need to make a note for the record that evidently the witness testified, line 7 -- 22, 7, it appears he said -- I'm sorry, 22, 4, it appears he said "in a small valley." Thank you. "In a small valley where my cousin laid down, having a grenade --" I'm sorry, "it was better" -- I'll start over. Line 22, 3. "He said that it was better for us to be killed," at least that's what the transcript reflects, and I'm just informed that he said, "it was better for us to commit suicide." So I just want to make that note for the record, or to ask the witness again to just repeat what was their intent with respect to the grenade. I think there's a difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, have you just heard what Ms. Richardson has just said? And if you have, do you agree with her that that is the case, in other words, that your relative suggested that it was better to commit suicide rather than be captured alive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Both of us said so, and we had these grenades ready there to kill ourselves. But as it turned out, he probably accidentally activated the grenade, killing himself, wounding me, and resulting in my capture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed, Ms. Richardson, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said you were wounded, could you tell us what kind of injuries you received as a result of that grenade explosion?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I was wounded in my face and hands, and it all turned numb. I was unable to get out of this stitch I was in. And as I managed to pull myself out, they started kicking me, swearing at me. At one point there was this sudden silence, and one of them shouted, "Should we kill him?" Others said, "No, let's not kill him, because what will the boss say," or what will someone else say. It was two or three times that they said, "What will Naser say," and then what will someone else say. And this is something I heard repeatedly during -- while I was actually captured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know at that time who the boss, or who Naser, they were referring to?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: No, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the people who captured you, how many soldiers, or I guess I should ask, were they dressed in uniforms?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes. I've already said they had different kinds of uniforms. Some wore camouflage, but some wore civilian clothes. They had all kinds of clothes on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many of them were there at that point when you were captured?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: At first, before my cousin was killed, when I looked out of the valley, believing that I would spot someone in Maltasi and try to get in touch, I looked at the road, at the crossroads to Maltasi and further down to Dvizovici. There was a large group of people. I couldn't exactly count them, but I reckon there were at least 150 people there, including young women specifically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that time were you able to -- and they were all -- they all had weapons? Were you also able to see whether or not they had radios?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes, they had radios. Once I was captured, at one point they said, "What's the time? We must tell the boss what time exactly this man was captured," which was at 1445 hours exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell whether or not -- could you see if they were using those radios?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what kind of radio it was that they -- that you observed them carrying? Could you describe it to us, if you don't know the exact type of radio?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I couldn't give you the type or the brand. They had radio communication with antennae, that sort of thing. They carried something else on their backs, possibly, but I couldn't -- I was not able to turn around and look at exactly what they had and what they used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one other question with respect to the uniforms. Could you tell -- could you tell us if they were wearing anything on their heads?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I noticed, in the place where I was captured, two or three different distinguishing features that they had. They had some sort of headband, they had armbands. Two, three different kinds of insignia were used. The ribbons were red and blue, light blue. Later on, I realised, based on this, that they probably came together from a number of different directions where they had been attacking different villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they wearing -- and again, with respect to my question about whether or not they were wearing anything on their head, were they wearing a beret or caps or anything that you noticed?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes. They wore green berets with lilies on them. But not all of them. I must be honest about this, not all of them. There were some young men who were wearing this sort of cap and some who were not. Red, that sort of thing. See my point?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I'd like to take you back to -- at the point where you were taken out of the depression or you were captured, could you tell us Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. what happened to you after you were removed from this depression, and could you tell us how it was that you actually came out of the depression itself? Were you able to climb out on your own or were you assisted?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: They simply ordered me. I was barely able to move. The depression was not that deep. I tumbled over and fell down onto the road. And once I was at the road, one of them kicked me and another man hit me with a rifle butt. One spat at me and one slapped me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened after that? Did they take you anywhere?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes. That was after they had talked and asked about the time in order to know when exactly the Chetnik was captured. They lingered on for a minute or two, and then we headed out towards a forest near Kolari. We passed a cemetery. There's a meadow, a clearing in the woods, and there were already women there, sitting in a circle. The group also included a young boy. I was not really able to watch. I just sort of saw the scene in passing. I spotted a group of women with this child. We passed them and continued on to Kolari. They helped me along for a while until I grew completely -- until my numbness was completely gone and I was able to walk on on my own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The group that you saw, the woman and the small boy, did you know, did you recognise anyone in the group? And could you tell us if they were Serb or Muslim?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: They were Serbs. I knew all of them by sight. But I was heading down the Drina River and they were headed in the opposite direction. I recognised this young boy, Mitrovic. I recognised most of their faces to the extent that I could get a really good look, because I only saw them in passing. But I couldn't give you their names. I couldn't tell you what the difference is between their respective names, if you understand what I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The small boy, you said his last name was Mitrovic. Is that Branimir Mitrovic, also known as Branko?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes, Branimir Mitrovic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that they were standing in a group. Could you tell us, other than the women and the small boy, who else was in this group?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Not standing. They were seated, if you see what I mean. I said several times that I knew those people, but I don't think it would mean anything to you if I started explaining now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition -- they were civilians; correct?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice --

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: -- civilians. Those were ladies that had been forced to leave their homes and taken to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Forced by whom? And I guess my question is: Was there anyone else standing with them, any men in uniform or civilian clothing --

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Well, yes --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- I guess I should say sitting.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The men in uniform and civilian clothing, were they armed?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Well, I hope the idea you're getting is not those mothers who had been inside their homes were also carrying weapons. Those were just housewives peacefully going about on their own business in their own homes and that was when they were picked up and taken to Srebrenica. That's what I was able to see as we were passing the group. There were, I think, about two soldiers standing by the group. Whether they were guarding the group or just passing by, like we were, I don't know. Anyway, I later heard that they too were brought in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So from what you could see, it didn't appear to you as though the women and the small boy, Branko, were free to leave, that they were being guarded?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: No. No. Certainly not. Had they been able to, they would have -- well, yes, they would have left their homes. They wouldn't have been there, under escort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us about the road that you took, and if anything significant happened after you passed the small group, which included the boy Branko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, on the road to Kolari, I was ahead of them. They gave me a rifle. They said, "There was a Chetnik who wants to fight us." And we reached a place called Stencica, the forest of Borovnik. There are blackberries growing there. I found Damjan Maksimovic there. I later found out that it was him. He was probably trying to escape from them. Suddenly, there was an explosion, a grenade exploded, and he killed himself right there. And when the explosion occurred, they started shooting. When they passed his body, they just turned the body over, extracting a pack of cigarettes from one of his pockets. That was all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many soldiers were escorting you, walking along with you?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: In order to be realistic, I really can't tell you exactly how many. I can talk about the number of soldiers when I was captured, but I -- while I was still ahead of them, I was in no position to be turning back. I could hear the sound of boots stomping on the ground, but I couldn't tell how many. They were after me, they were following me on the road to Kolari. And we walked down to a water -- a small water plant in Kolari. And one man came along and he said that he would give me some heat, meaning probably that he would kill me. He brought me over to a bramble tree, and then another man came along and said, "Don't touch him? What will the man say?" And then they took me back to towards Radovcici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened after you were taken in that direction?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: We were moving in that direction until we reached a village further on from Radovcici. An elderly lady came out, and she said, "Listen, Chetnik, you killed my grandson," and then she started -- started hitting out at me with a pair of metal tongs or a poker used to poke coal, embers. I had never been to that village before, therefore I didn't know what she was talking about, but I can't deny that something like that might have happened in that village anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the soldiers prevent her from hitting you, the ones that were escorting you?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: She hit out at me several times, and then we left the village and headed for Kragljevode.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happens after you arrived in Kragljevode?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I'll say this again. When we reached the village, the name of which I think is Tokoljac, the soldiers stayed right there and I was escorted by a young man and young woman with automatic weapons who took me to Kragljevode. At that time a lorry came along. We boarded the lorry and were off to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The young man and woman who carried automatic weapons, were they also dressed as soldiers? Or, I should say, were they in uniform or civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes. Uniform. Uniform. The young woman, I can't remember specifically, but I do believe she also wore a camouflage jacket over jeans or something like that. The young man was wearing a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And once you were -- you were put into a lorry; correct?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was in this lorry? Or were there any other individuals in this lorry?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: In this lorry, apart from the three of us, the two of them and myself, there were two -- four or five, actually, other soldiers also carrying weapons, and some persons who were wounded, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said there were persons wounded, who were you referring to? Were they wounded civilians or wounded --

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they of Serb or Muslim ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Muslim, and they were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you the only Serb civilian in the lorry?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what, if anything, happened during the -- while you were in the lorry being taken to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: As we got onto the lorry, this young man said, "Here's a Chetnik. We need to take him to Srebrenica." They started lighting matches, one by one, to see if I could identify them. I said I couldn't, I said I didn't know them. Some hit me, some spat at me, some made threats that they would cut one of my limbs once we arrived in the prison. And it went on like that until we reached Srebrenica eventually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time of day did you arrive in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: It was dark by that time. I'm not sure about the exact time, but darkness was already present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to this day, January 16th, 1993, had you been to Srebrenica before?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I'd been to Srebrenica on business several times, when I needed to get a new ID or when I went for military -- premilitary training, but that was all. I never needed to go there for any other reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once you arrived in Srebrenica, what happened?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Once we were there, across the way from the department store, those two persons, the young man and woman who brought me, I heard the man's name was Cicko Mevludin, but I can't confirm whether that was the person. He asked me whether I would give him my clothes and watch, the watch that I had on me, as well as my boots. I didn't have a choice, really, so I said that I would.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just before we discuss what was -- what you -- what clothing -- your clothing and your watch, could you tell us where the truck or the lorry stopped in Srebrenica? Could you identify whether it was in front of a building or some other structure?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: There was a building, coming from the direction of Jadar, and the department store is to your right. I can't tell you if this was a social security building, or something like that. But I could see a young woman coming down the stairs, and she brought me a pair of slippers after my boots had been taken from me, a pair of women's slippers, very small, and some sort of an overall, which was blue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the material of this overall? Was it thin or thick material?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Blue. Thin, just perfectly regular overall. I think they use the same kind all over the world. Maybe the colour differs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after these items were taken from you, what happened next?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Next, they took me to the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "they," who are you referring to? And how many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I can't tell you. It was night, and I remember this same man, Cicko, after a while, they told me that the person weighs name was Mevludin. My conclusion was his name was Cicko Mevludin. She walked ahead of me, and there was someone walking behind, but I didn't turn back. And we reached the police station. They took me to a cell there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we get to what happened in the police station, could you tell me whether these individuals were wearing uniforms? And were these the same individuals that were in the truck or the lorry?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Well, when I reached the police station, this young man and woman were no longer around, or at least I couldn't see them. Once there, there were police officers who were wearing blue uniforms, the kind they used to wear in the former Yugoslavia. Outside there were, perhaps, two officials, and inside there were about four or five persons, not including the one who had brought me there. I can't tell you whether anyone else was around, but I did notice one particular person whom I had seen previously, before my arrival in Srebrenica. He's a rather tall man. He had a white cotton coat with black spots. My idea was that the man's name was Nurija, but I can't be sure about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were taken to the police station, were you taken directly to Nurija, or were you -- prior to being taken some place else in the building? And where was this Nurija located? Was he in a particular area of the building?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Nurija was standing in the hallway of the police station, and he asked me, "Chetnik, do you know Pero Milosevic?" And I said, "Yes, he is my wife's uncle." My apologies for this obscenity. He said, "I'll fuck his mother. He's a Chetnik just like you are."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after he said this to you, did he ask you any questions about yourself, or anything else, for that matter?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: After that they seized my wallet. My military identification booklet was there as well as other personal documents. Probably a photograph of my wife and a photograph of myself. Some money was probably in the wallet too. They made some remarks and then took me along to the cell, to the right of the entrance to the police station. Once I was just outside the cell, they opened the door. One of them kicked me in the small of my back, and I banged my head against a radiator, as a result of which I fell unconscious.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The person who kicked you, could you see -- could you tell what he was wearing? Was it a uniform or civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: It was probably a uniform. But again, it was nighttime, there was no electricity, no light, no nothing. See my point? I wasn't exactly there for a field day. I wasn't looking around. Once I was pushed inside the room, he hit me from behind. As I was falling, I banged my head against the radiator, and I just fell unconscious.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were -- when you were -- when you struck your head, do you remember if there was any blood as a result, or any kind of injury to your head?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I was bleeding. The next morning, before they beat me again, I realised that I was all covered in blood. Maybe it was as a result of the wounding, too, and not only banging my head. I was suffering severe pain. And I also saw blood on the other people in the room before I hit my head against the radiator. I can't tell you whether those other people in the cell too had been beaten, or whether the blood was all mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other people in the cell, how many were there, that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Kojo was in the cell, a man nicknamed Kojo. Then there was Mico. I did say this several times. I'm not sure if Mile Trifunovic was also there, but I'm sure that he was brought the next day. There were two or three people. I can't say exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just going over the names of these individuals again. You said there was -- did you know any of these individuals prior to meeting them in this cell?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: No, with the exception of Mile. I can't remember, but he probably came the next day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember Mile's last name? Did he have --

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes, Trifunovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the other individuals, what were their names? Do you remember -- do you remember their names? Did they tell you at some point?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I didn't know at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you later --

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I found out later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could you tell us what the names are? In addition to Mile Trifunovic, could you tell us the other individuals?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, Kojo was there, Ratko was there too, and Mico, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I think it's a good point to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Richardson. We'll have a 25-minute break, starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, before the break, you were testifying to the men who were also in the same cell as you were placed in, and I'd like to clarify with you the names of those individuals. The first question is: How many -- how many, including yourself, were kept in this prison, in this cell? How many men?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there were four of us altogether, if I remember well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. If I can just have a moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall giving the names of the men that were kept in the cell with you to the Prosecution -- or to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I remember that with me in the cell was Ratko Nikolic. That's something I learnt later. Vojo, nicknamed Kostadin, and Vico Sasje, if I remember well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to Vico, do you know how his last name to be Bogdan?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did say at the outset that I would object to the Prosecution suggesting names to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think I will sustain the objection, and you will need to rephrase your question, whichever way you can rephrase it, now that you have already pronounced the name.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At least try to --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: -- I'll try to rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall giving the name of an additional individual, an additional name, to the investigator, and that being the name of one of the men that you were held with?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Let me try and remember now. I don't know, perhaps I might have mixed up the hospital with the prison cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the name that you gave to the investigator as Bogdan?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in the cell with you, so we're clear, is an individual called Ratko, Kosta, Bogdan, and Mile Trifunovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: No. I mentioned Mile Trifunovic several times, but he was not with me at that point. He only came in the following day, as far as I can remember, and I think that's what I've been telling in my statement. I hope that I did not make any mistakes there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So for the first night, for the first time that you became aware that there were other men in that cell with you, these other men were Ratko, Kosta, and Bogdan?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at some point, Mile Trifunovic was also brought to the cell.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes. That was the following morning, at the latest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe the cell that you were held in with these other men.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I will describe it to you the way I could see it. I don't know if it's necessary for me to describe what the building looked like the moment we entered the police station, or just the cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, had you been to this building before, before being -- before January 16th, this particular building?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I went to that station only once, when I needed to get my identity card, and never again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were aware that evening, when you were brought there, that that was the police station?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: It was already nighttime, and I could only assume it was the police station building. But because there were police officers there, and when we got into the reception hall in the lobby, on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And could you describe for us the cell that you were kept in. Could you tell us the measurement? Was it big, small? Did it have a window? And other things that might be important.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, at the very entrance to the cell, there were these bars. It was actually a barred window. And I could see nothing of the cell itself, because it was nighttime. The following morning, at dawn, I noticed that there was a radiator there and a window that was closer to the ceiling, opposite the door that -- through which I got into the cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this radiator, was that the one that you struck your head on, that -- when you were -- when the person kicked you into the cell?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Most probably, because that's something I inferred from how my head hit against the radiator.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was this a metal radiator?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Most probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of floor did this cell have?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: As far as I could see, it was a concrete floor. The following morning, when I came to after this hit in the head, I could see people lying on the floor. There was no heating and not any sort of carpeting on the floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the temperature in the room?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Probably the same as outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the following morning, were you able to determine if there were any beds or blankets in the room?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: No, there was none of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it when you say the temperature was the same as outside, are you -- was it cold outside?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes, it was. It was wintertime, and Srebrenica is a similar -- a similarly placed settlement as my own village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: At this time, Your Honour, I would like to have the usher's assistance with an exhibit that will be shown to the witness. And we need to have it -- a number assigned to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which exhibit are we talking about, Ms. --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: We're talking about a sketch of a building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, it's with the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: There are two.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Just the first one, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is the one which has ERN number finishing with 1400.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, I would like to have the witness -- Your Honour, I'm sorry, I'd actually like to have the witness view the sketch that ends in ERN number 401.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That's why I mentioned it, because the registrar mentioned or drew your attention that there were two, and you said the first one, and the first one, according to -- at least numerically would be 400, not 401. But there is absolutely no problem with using 401 before 400.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: We'll get to the second exhibit in a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, do you recall when you were interviewed by the investigator for the Prosecutor that you described the first building you were held in when you arrived in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you prepare a sketch, an outline, of the inside of that building as it appeared to you at that time?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I drew this sketch that wasn't as nice as this one. But this one is an accurate reflection of my own sketch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the sketch that's before you, Prosecution Exhibit number -- I'm not sure if a number was assigned to it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not yet. This will receive Exhibit Number P473, P473.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, P473, is a sketch, as you stated, of the building that you were held in when you first arrived in Srebrenica. Does this sketch reflect the one that you drew originally?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you, in fact, reviewed this sketch, and you signed your name?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes, I most certainly did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you could --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: If I could have the usher's assistance to place this sketch, Prosecution's Exhibit 473, on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, I'd like you to take a look at that sketch now, and walk us through via your testimony, where it was that you first entered the building, by pointing -- if -- okay.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. For the record, the witness indicates or points to the spot on the document where it says "Main Entrance Door," "Vrata," and also Glavni Vlaz.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you came in that way, so what Your Honour just placed on the record. Where was it that you spoke to, or you were questioned when you first entered the building? Could you point to that area?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: [Indicates]. Yes, it's this area here, where I said that the men who first asked me about what I'd been telling about before was called Nurija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this happened in the corridor, in the hallway, in other words? Not inside the room.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, it was in the corridor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So for the record, the witness points at the triangle that is situated or is shown above the reception room, in the same document, in which a triangle there is the word "door" and partly in, partly out, the word "Vrata." Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, Mr. Ivanovic, where it was that the cell you were held in was located? Could you point to it on the --

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes, I will. [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. For the record, the witness points at the square at the extreme top right of the diagram, in which there is the word "cell," "celija". Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on that sketch as well, could you point to where, inside the room, you remember the radiator being located?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The witness, for the record, points at the part in that -- the spot in that room which already indicates "radiator."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also, could you point to where the door to that cell was located, and the bars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, let's cut this -- that room, as shown in this diagram, shows a radiator. It shows a door. It shows a hallway door, vrata, a hallway us the room. It shows cell bars, and it shows also where a bucket is supposed to have been located. Are all these things and places correctly indicated in that room, or not? In that sketch.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only thing I can't remember about is this bucket, because there's a bucket drawn here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But otherwise, the door to the small corridor and the door, then, from that small corridor that leads to the main corridor, are as shown in the diagram? Do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm not sure whether this was a door, but I know that you would go into the corridor and then you would come across the bars and then you would have the door, just as it is drawn here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Were there any windows in this cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There was a window placed higher up, toward the ceiling, and it was smaller.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where was it in relation to the radiator? Was it above the radiator? Was it on that wall, or was it on a different wall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have to believe me when I tell you that I simply did not have the time to pay attention to these things. But I can tell you that I assume that it was halfway up, something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but was it on the wall where there was the radiator, or was it on another wall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It was above the radiator, as far as I remember, if I remember well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ivanovic. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ivanovic, do you recall how many -- were there guards guarding you at this point, you and the other prisoners, as you were held in the cell?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there were none that I could see there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there individuals -- when you say "there," what do you mean by "there"? There was no one, there were no guards directly outside of your cell. Maybe we can go back to the diagram. The door to your cell, the hallway door, or outside the bars, there was no one there guarding you?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Precisely so. I could not see anyone just outside the cell. I only saw those who came to beat us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us about the beatings that occurred in the cell? How often were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I don't know, because many times I would slip out of consciousness. But I do remember this once, when a man came to beat me, he ordered me to come close to the bars, grabbed my ears, and then slipped his hand through the bars, hitting me in the face, calling me names, a Chetnik's mother. And then he motioned as if he was going to pluck my eye out, saying "That Chetnik doesn't need to have eyes."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall how this individual was dressed, what he was wearing?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I've said this several times already. I think that it was either a camouflage uniform or those were civilian clothes. I can't really say. I was beaten so many times; I was covered in blood. The only thing that I could notice was that he was a tall man. I noticed this while he was beating me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did other people beat you as well, other than this particular individual?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
