utterances.text: They would come and go. It wasn't always the same person coming. I suppose that those who were their superiors allowed them to do so. Some would come and beat me with rods. It was perhaps easiest for them to just poke the rods through the bars and then hit me in the head, in the shoulders. And that's how they would do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one small matter. I've noticed this witness does have a tendency sometimes to speculate and to say that "probably X" or he supposes Y. Perhaps he could be instructed that he's only to tell us, of course, what he knows. There he's supposing that superiors allowed them to do something. If it's not within his knowledge, perhaps he can be instructed that he should just tell us what he knows. I've noticed several examples so far, and I thought it was time to bring it to your attention.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think this is necessary. I think the witness is simply saying how he believed this occurred. So I don't think he's at all speculating. I'm sure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the time, for whatever it may be worth, I think it can be accepted as it is being put. Then obviously you have a right to ask him whether he is speculating or whether he has at least some basic ground on which he is basing his assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I can, of course, cover all these points in cross-examination. It was just that I thought it might save time if this witness is clear from the start that if he doesn't know something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think I can suggest even to my colleagues that we consider this as mere, pure speculation. At this point in time, he's telling us what his assessment was at the time, and what supposedly it is still now. And then we cover it as we go along.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I don't think it's being put as mere speculation as such, okay? Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that you were beaten. Were the other prisoners beaten as well?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: May I just say one more thing? I hope that the Honourable Judge does not think that I would pretend to know what these people thought. I wasn't on friendly terms there with them, to know what was going on in their heads.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, with respect to my question about the beatings of other prisoners, could you tell us whether or not they were also beaten, along with yourself?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes, they beat them as well, but they beat me most. I spent most of the time in sort of a coma, so it's very difficult for me to explain it all to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did they use to beat you and the other prisoners? You mentioned rods. Could you tell us whether that was a metal or wooden rod, and if they used any other types of items?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: These were metal rods. There were some wooden bats, baseball bats, as they call them. Whatever could be poked through the bars was used. And they did beat the other ones as well, but probably to a lesser extent, although I don't really remember everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The beatings that occurred, could you -- were these beatings done by men who were guarding you? Do you know who these men were?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I couldn't really say that it was the guards who beat us, because if they had beat us, they would probably have opened the door, whereas the people who did beat us would do it through the bars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mentioned, you testified, about an incident with a knife. Could you tell us a little bit more about that, with a knife and your eyelid? Could you tell us a little bit more about this?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, I did say that. Much in the same he showed me, he beckoned me, "Chetnik, come over here," I came as far as the bars, and then he poked a knife through the bars, pointing it at my eyes saying that a Chetnik will not need an eye. It is purely coincidental that I was not hurt. There were no injuries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain how it was that your head was struck against the bars of the cell? Could you explain that in further detail?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Why not. I've said it already. They would put their hands through the bars, grab me by the ears and then bang my head against the bars until I fell unconscious.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to the incident with your -- with the knife being held against your eye, did there come a time that you were threatened with a knife in addition to that time? Were any threats made to cut off your hand, for instance?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I don't remember that specifically. That was in a different cell. But I'll say this again: I can't quite remember, but I think it was also the police station. He tried to cut my arm when I held my hand out. I don't remember whether it was in the prison or elsewhere. But I do believe that it was, after all, at the police station, in the prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of injuries did you receive as a result of the beatings? Could you tell us what your physical condition was?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Which point in time do you have in mind? While I was at the police station or ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll clarify. At this point in time we're talking about at the police station and my question is: What was your physical condition following the beatings at the police station?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: My physical condition was very poor at the police station. I was beaten until I fell unconscious, and so were the other people. We would lie on the floor with no mattress or blankets, food or water. I don't know what else I can say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you bleeding, or were the others bleeding?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes, I've said that, didn't I? I was all covered in blood, and I assume that some of the others were covered in my blood, as I was in theirs. We were all covered in blood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time of the day or evening did the beatings occur, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I do remember. I think it always happened, for the most part, just before dusk, and at night too. You could say from the onset of dusk on, whenever it occurred to someone to do so, they would beat us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you treated, you or any of the other prisoners, treated for injuries as a result of the beating?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: No, never, not in any way, in neither of the cells. Never. The first treatment I received was at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any food or water while you were in this building?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you held in this cell, you and the other prisoners? Well, I should rephrase that question. How long were you held in this cell?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I said it several times, when asked. I believe two, three, or four days, as a maximum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a point in time that you were removed, you and the other prisoners were removed from this cell?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes. After those two, three, or four days - I wasn't counting at the time - we were taken to the All People's Defence building. I think in the former Yugoslavia it used to be between the court building and the town hall, the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, before we leave the police station altogether, I have a final question for you: Did you speak to the other prisoners who were there, and did they tell you how long they had been held in that cell prior to your arrival?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. At this point I'd like you to tell us about the transfer of yourself and the other prisoners from this police building to the -- the defence building. When did this occur? What time of the day?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I think it was in the afternoon. Two soldiers took us there, I can't remember how. I only remember how I arrived in the cell at the All People's Defence building. I can't even remember how I was transferred there, or whether I was barefoot or actually had shoes on. It's difficult to form an image in my mind now. I remember that moment, and a while later I remember myself already been transferred to a different cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember if you were -- if you walked or if you had been taken there in a vehicle? Do you recall that much?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I really can't remember. That's precisely what I told you about the footwear. I simply don't remember. I remember that later on, I was in a different cell which was different from the one in which I had previously been held.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you and all -- and the other prisoners transferred to this other building together?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Probably so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone come to you and say anything to you about the transfer, just before you were actually removed from the police building; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: No, or at least not that I remember. Someone probably picked us up. But how, and using what exactly, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you were escorted by soldiers. Do you remember how many?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I remember that I said probably two soldiers, but I underlined at the time that I was not able to form an accurate image of this, whether we Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. were brought there walking or in a different way. I remember finding myself in a different room a while later. I remember that it was no longer the same room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall, prior to your being held in this building, whether you had been to this building before, during the times in the past when you had visited Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Whether I ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this the first -- I'll rephrase the question. Was this the first time you had been in this building, the national defence building?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you describe to us what happened when you arrived at the building, if you recall, you and the other prisoners.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: The moment I arrived, I was probably not fully conscious of everything that was going on; therefore, I can't remember everything. But later, when I was taken to see a judge in the town hall, I had a different view of the entrance, the one that I've already described, as well as the cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall any other -- well, could you -- I'll rephrase. Could you describe the cell that you were placed in.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Of course I can. After everything that had happened, and when I regained consciousness, at the entrance to the building, to the right and then straight down, at the front of that building, there was a prison three, three by four, or something like that. I can't say exactly. Probably to my right there were two windows, maybe more. But I remember two. At the entrance of the door itself, we were lying there in a circle. Outside the door there was a table with two or three chairs. Mile Trifunovic sat in one of those chairs. I remember well that I was considering the possibility of hanging myself if they started cutting me up. There were two pipes with two valves above that table.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall if there were any beds or blankets in the room?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: No, certainly not. What beds? Some blankets on the floor, one blanket for two persons, and there was another blanket to cover ourselves with. But this meant nothing, because after they had beaten us, they would poor water on us and then kick us to see whether we were still alive, and then this same routine again. And they would just smile.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall if there was a window in that room?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He has already said that there were two that he can remember, maybe more, but he doesn't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He can perhaps confirm whether there was a stove in that room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honour's question was whether or not there was a stove in the room. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes, there was a stove, which wasn't much use. They would make a fire several times. One of those people, guards or soldiers, or whoever they were, they would fill the stove, and then an hour later they would come to our door to say, "Look at all these Chetniks, they're still alive."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were you aware of whether or not there were other rooms close to -- in the vicinity of your cell?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What rooms do you recall?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I suppose there was a room to the left of our cell, that it was empty, whereas in the one next to that, there were the women and children who were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall if there was a toilet?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes, there was a toilet. I can only speak for myself, of course. In the 40 days I spent there, I only went once. Ratko Nikolic helped me. There was a boot that was cut in half, and I used that to relieve myself. I'm not sure what he did then. But I know that he told me, "Ilija, don't go anywhere. If you leave this room, you will never come back alive." I had no need to go, really, because I hardly had any food or anything to drink, and what I had was precious little.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Getting back to the room, the description of the room, could you tell us whether or not you remember whether the window that you described or recall had glass? And can you tell us whether or not the room was warm or cold, what the temperature was?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: The same thing applies as to the SUP building. The temperature was more or less the same as outside temperature. Sometimes they would light a fire for us, but it didn't give any heat at all. And then sometimes, after making this fire, they would try to stop up the window, there would be a pane of glass that was broken, and then one and a half hours later they would try to stop it up, and then an hour and a half or two later, they would be back just to say, "Look at these Chetniks, they are still alive."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would request the usher's assistance with the next exhibit, and that is the document ending in 400, which is a sketch as well. And if we can have a number assigned to this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This would be P474. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, please take a look at that sketch, and I would ask you the same questions I asked before about the previous exhibit and the sketch that you testified to. Do you recall providing information about the way the building -- the area where you were held appeared to you when you were in prison in Srebrenica, the national defence building, that is?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: That's true. I have it in front of me. And if you want me to, I can explain to you what this is about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. For the moment I would only ask you with respect to the sketch: Is this the sketch that you yourself drew, or is this a sketch that was drawn from your sketch?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: That's correct. The sketch that I drew was altered. But I signed this new one and it accurately reflects what I had drawn in the first place. If you want me to, I can show it to you --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: -- the way that I originally drew it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, why don't you tell us whether this sketch accurately reflects that when you walk into the building there is a hallway, and to the right there is a reception room. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I do. That's correct. What is drawn here is perfectly accurate. Actually, it was drawn by me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you point to where your cell was located.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. For the record, the witness indicates the section of the diagram which contains the word "cell" and "celija," and the right-hand side -- at the right-hand side of the document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And looking at the sketch, do you recall that there was a table located approximately where this is -- this is drawn on the sketch? And also look at the area where a stove was located. Does that fairly represent the room as you remembered it?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: That is true. But the table, as far as I can remember, the table was just opposite the door which was opposite the entrance, and there were two or three chairs around it. The stove was in this area over here, give or take a metre or two. And the window was one of these. [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. For the record, the witness indicates the windows, the stove, and the table as indicated, or as shown in the diagram, and confirms that they were in the same position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, also on this diagram, there is a -- can you see -- could you confirm for us that, in fact, this is where the women's room was located, where the women were held in this building?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's correct. I can point it out to you, the room in which the women were being held. [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. For the record, the witness indicates the square on the diagram which contains the words "women's room," zenska soba.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the toilet that you recall was located next to your cell? And is that correctly reflected in the diagram before you?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes, it's correctly reflected, but not the door. I remember clearly the door to the cell was over here, as far as I can remember. [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the record should reflect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, so let me understand. Where was the door to the toilets? Can you show it on the diagram.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Indicates]. [Interpretation] I showed that it was here, because I knew it was just next to the door to the cell, to the left of the door, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's get this clear. If you look at that diagram, you see already a door plotted there; right? That is the door of the cell; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the door of the cell where -- was where it is shown on the diagram?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I remember that it was straight down the corridor and to the right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And next to it, in the wall of the room that you describe as toilets, there was a door leading to the toilets. And that would be at exactly adjacent to the door leading to the cell. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Can I finally ask you, sir, to take a pen and draw on that diagram the place -- indicate to us the place where the door to the toilets was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try to show everything, to the extent that I remember. [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And while we are at it, could you also indicate where the door leading to the reception, the "prijavnica," was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand what you're asking, you mean the way out, or you mean the door to the reception room?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The door to the reception room.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll show it right here. [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Could you plot it on the diagram, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And the door leading to the woman's room, the zenska soba.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please put your initials against each of those three doors, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivanovic. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, when you arrived at this prison, this cell, were there other prisoners there?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time that other prisoners were, in fact, brought in?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: That's correct. They were brought in from Cerska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall the names of the individuals that were brought in?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes, I remember their names, I've said several times, after my captivity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many men were brought in?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Four men and one woman were brought in from Cerska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, prior to -- do you recall the names of these individuals, and could you tell us their names?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I'll do my best. Rade Pejic. Dragan Ilic. Andza, I didn't know her last name. Branko Sekulic. I can't remember. If I may be allowed to use the piece of paper that I have brought over from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is this piece of paper that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: This is something that Milomir Djukic wrote down for me at the hospital. He asked all of us who were there at the hospital, should any of us survive, to ascertain exactly who were the people at the hospital, and in the prison previously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You recall speaking with the investigator about the men that were brought in from Cerska.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall, but I may need a bit of time, because there were so many things I'm thinking about at the same time. I do know the man well, though, all of them in fact, all three of them, and I could describe them for you too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, do you recall telling the investigators that Jakov Djukic was also brought in from Cerska?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you in the prison before the others arrived from Cerska?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I believe about 17 days, give or take a day or two. I did not exactly keep count. It's just how it seemed at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall who brought them to the prison, if they were escorted by any one when they were brought to your cell?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Escorted, yes. But we had been beaten so badly, and I did not even dare turn around. I was in a very poor state. And what I did manage to see was a brief glance over my shoulder, that was all. Once they were inside the cell, they started beating them, like they had beaten us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to other people in the cell, do you recall if at some point other men were brought to the cell, other individuals, in addition to the people from Cerska?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I don't remember those who were brought in. And following my captivity, this man Miloje came. Miloje, Cane, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you recall giving the names --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Again, we don't want the Prosecution to be feeding names to the witness. If the witness can just try to recall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness has asked me to refer to this piece of paper, that we authorise him, and we will look at it --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry, I'll repeat. The witness -- alternatively, the witness will ask me to refer to this piece of paper that he says he received, indicating all the names, containing all the names, and of course we will have to authorise him if he does that, and it will get us back to where you don't want to arrive. I mean, let's be practical about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm interested in being practical, by all means. It's just that there are certain individuals who really -- we really don't know, and I believe the witness doesn't know, their first name, their last name. The danger is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not going to change.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The danger is the Prosecution will use one of these other documents or some other source to suggest a name to the witness, and so we're not getting his evidence, we're getting the Prosecution's version of who these people were. That's my fear.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at some point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: -- The witness did learn the names of certain individuals, and I believe he can testify to that. He can also testify as to whether or not he knew the names or not, or never learned it. And certainly he can testify about whether or not these are the individuals that he is referring to. And certainly at this point, we can ask the witness if there's anything that would refresh his memory as to who was held in this prison with him, and this is in reference to the piece of paper that he mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. This is what I referred -- Mr. Ivanovic, are you having problems with remembering the names of these individuals who were in the same cell with you, or in the same building with you, there in the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm not. It's just that it all gets mixed up, and at the point when I have to give you the last names, I just can't. It's not that I don't know these people. I know all the men that were with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we be of any help to you? How can we help you to refresh your memory and be more precise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. Perhaps if you just gave me a name, and then I can tell you yes or no. Otherwise, it would take me a bit longer to try and visualise them all as they were lying down in the cell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And you said you have a piece of paper which, at some time, at some point in time, you hinted you would like to refer to, this paper that was given to you by Djukic, or whatever his name is. Do you have it with you here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. I have the paper. I copied it before my departure. And I'm sorry that I actually didn't bring the original paper with me. It's already all tore up. Because Milomir Djukic, as he wrote the names on the piece of paper, he rolled it up like a cigarette. And then I put it under my underwear, because I really wanted to guard it well. And then as I returned to the cell, I placed it beneath the linoleum that was there. And then I also tried to hide the piece of paper behind the pipes that were running along the ceiling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And do you think that by referring to this piece of paper it will help you to remember better the names of these persons? Would you like to refer to this piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, unless you would object to that, because if you would object to that, then it would take me a bit longer to remember them. Otherwise I can read the piece of paper that I have with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So what I suggest to you, in order to help you, is the following: That you produce this piece of paper, on which you say you have these names, you let us have a look at it, that means the Defence, Prosecution, and ourselves, and then you can refresh your memory by referring to this piece of paper. Let's see it, to start with. And I will ask you a couple of questions on it as well. Show it to the Prosecution and to the Defence. Yes, the understanding is that the witness will make use of this document, after I put a couple of questions to him. Then when he's finished with that document, we will have it photocopied so that we keep a record of it, and you will have a record of it and you will have a record of it, all right?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. When did you prepare that list? When did you write that list on the piece of paper, on that piece from a diary, a paper, a sheet from a diary, that it is on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This piece of paper here, that I brought with me here, is a copy of the list that was contained on that other paper that I brought from captivity and that I had in Srebrenica. Now, if you want me to, I can read out the names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When did you copy it? When?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just before my departure for The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And this other list, the original, have you shown it to the investigators, to the Office of the Prosecutor, or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have. Eileen Gilleece, if I've pronounced her name and surname well, she was there. And perhaps you won't believe me when I tell you this, but I also brought with me a list of names of people who used to live with me in the village, because you see my memory fails me. And I just wanted to have it there in case. But if you don't want me to, I won't read the names on this particular list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have a copy of the original, by any chance, in your records?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, no, as far as I know, we do not have a copy of the original list. However, I will seek to determine that further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Ivanovic, do you confirm or note, do you swear that this is a faithful copy of the original, in other words, that it contains no more and no less and nothing different from what the original contains?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assure you that this is an accurate copy. And if you want to, you can have someone visit my home. It's there, the list, in the pocket of my jacket. My wife is there at home. She could check in my purse. I have two purses, and one of them contains this particular list. You will see what it's like. It's all chipped and torn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, when you go back home, please have that original photocopied and send it to Ms. Richardson, and then Ms. Richardson will let us have a copy of it. In the meantime, you are being authorised by us three to refer to that document to refresh your memory.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So perhaps you can answer the question which was, earlier on, put to you by Ms. Richardson, namely, we are only interested on knowing who was with you during your stay in the prison in Srebrenica. You can start by telling us who was with you, and go slowly because ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have set aside those who arrived in Cerska from those who were already there in the cell. The following were brought in from Cerska: Branko Sekulic, Jakov Djukic, Mico from Sase - I don't know his surname - Dragan Ilic, Rade Pejic, and Andza was the woman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Did you --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Did you see Mr. Milomir Djukic writing this document? Did you see him writing it or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did. I will tell you something more about him. This Djukic, apart from the two days that he spent in the cell, spent the entire time in the hospital. He was wounded in both his legs, and thanks to this physician there - I'd like to see him some day - his legs were saved. He was able to walk to the toilet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And can you tell us how he could procure a piece of paper and a writing instrument, a pen or a ball pen or pencil, whatever he wrote it with, while he was in detention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will explain it to you in detail. At a later stage, when I felt -- when he felt already better, he would receive comic books from the personnel there. Everyone respected him there. He told me that they had been beating him until the time he arrived in Srebrenica, where nobody was beating him. As far as he could tell me, he received all manner of assistance there. His legs were about to be amputated, but this particular physician suggested that they wait for a while. And his legs recovered, they were not amputated. And I'm very sorry that Milomir Djukic never showed up. I was organising a donation in Srebrenica, and I was talking to a man who was telling me that his brother was working for the police and he wanted to inquire after him, because he had heard that he died of some sort of a pulmonary disease, which I don't believe in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How did he come about a piece of paper and a pen, a writing instrument? Because I take it that while you were in detention, you were not allowed to keep anything with you. So how is it that this Mr. Djukic had a paper and also something to write with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You must have misunderstood me, although I didn't tell you everything in great detail. I expected you to ask me in stages. This was written in Srebrenica, at the hospital, and not in captivity, because I told you that Milomir Djukic was being brought old newspapers, comic books. So they really took great care of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So it wasn't written while he was in captivity, it was written while he was in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. He was in detention only for two days, but then again they sent him back to the hospital where I and others saw him, and where he wrote this down for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you see him in the hospital as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that's where you saw him writing it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. On one occasion, he said, "Let's make the list." And I assure you I was unable to move at the time. I was lying in a bed to the right from the entrance, and he was writing the list, asking people what their names were. And that's how this list before me was produced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, in addition to the men that were brought in from Cerska, which included Branko Sekulic and Dragan Ilic - I won't go through the others - and the men that were transferred with you from the police station, were there any other prisoners brought in during the time that you were held prison -- you were imprisoned in Srebrenica, the national defence building, that is?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes. There was Ratko Nikolic, then Kosta, nicknamed Kojo, Bogdan, Trifunovic Mile.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Another name that the interpreter hasn't caught.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall anyone else?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I believe I've mentioned them all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment, Mr. Ivanovic, because there is a small problem with the interpretation. You mentioned that there was Ratko Nikolic, then Kosta, nicknamed Kojo, Bogdan, and Trifunovic Mile, and you mentioned someone else but the interpreters couldn't catch up with you. Who was the other one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mile Radovanovic and Cane.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just for clarification, I believe you mentioned also before that a Miko was also in prison with you. Mico.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes, Mico from Sase.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Mico's name?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: No, I don't. I've never really known it, nor have I tried to find it out, because I'm just simply telling you what I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how old Mico was? You said he was from Sase. Do you recall his age?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Mico from Sase was born perhaps in 1950, 1952. It was difficult for me to make an accurate assessment. All of us were beaten up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mico, in addition to the fact that he was from Sase, did he tell you anything else about himself, or how it was that he was captured and brought to Srebrenica? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It was actually from someone else that I found out about this. When a person entered the cell and asked him where he had hidden the flour up there at the mine, and then he kept beating him in the chest and as a result of that he died. But I suppose we're going to go back to that later on, and then I'll be able to tell you the story exactly as I remember it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, we will get back to that. Now, you also testified that there were women in the prison.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes, there were women, but they were not held with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you -- from the diagram of the national defence building, you showed us on the map, on the sketch, where the women's room was. Could you tell us, how is it that you knew that women were being held there?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: At one point two soldiers came to us and told us that we had to go and bring some firewood for the stove. We somehow managed to get up and walk - I don't know how - and then we brought the firewood back. And it was then that I had occasion to see which room they were in, and see the door. That's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to hear them at all, hear them talking or anything else with respect to -- coming from that room?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: In those moments that I was conscious, I could hear a loud noise, whether it was moaning or some painful moans or something like that. I suppose we were beaten more often and more severely than the women; however, they would be the best ones to testify on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to the cell that you were kept in, you told us -- you testified earlier about the number of men that were there. Could you tell us exactly how many men were there altogether?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I think there were -- we were 14 altogether.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you able to -- how were you -- were you sleeping in the cell? Were you able to lie down?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes, we were. We were sleeping on the floor. It was a concrete floor that had some sort of a linoleum on it or something of the sort, that was torn into pieces, and blankets were spread over that. We would lie on them, to the right of the door -- from the door. It was only Mile Trifunovic who actually was there near a chair throughout his captivity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the period of time that you and the other prisoners were in this prison, were you given food or water?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I will describe this to you as well, although there was very little of that. I don't remember how many times we were given food; once or several times, I'm not sure. I don't want to exaggerate. It was difficult for me to know this. I was in very bad shape. I remember this once when a woman, a young woman, came to me and, as I was lying on my back, she simply placed it on my chest. The food consisted of this loaf of bread. Actually, it was just a small piece of bread. And then there was this soup, potato soup or bean soup. I don't know how much I could eat, but I know that it was for 40 days -- it was just once in these 40 days that I actually had to go to the toilet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I turn your attention to the beatings that you testified occurred. Could you tell us who beat you and the other prisoners, who it was?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I don't know their names. I only know about this one name that I heard of. As I've already said, the beatings would start after dusk, at 9 or 10 in the evening. When the soldiers would return from the battlefield, they would be driven in a truck, stop between the court and the police station -- in the municipality building. Then they would say, "Let's go and see the Chetniks." And they would beat us in any way they could, with whatever implements they had. I remember this once, when I was conscious, whenever they'd enter the room, they would shout out to Ratko, who was closest to the door, they would say, "Who is Ratko Mladic?" He would then raise two fingers, and then they wouldn't really bother noticing what it was that they used to hit him with, whether it was a rifle butt or a rod or something else. And then they would beat the rest of us as well, severely, all of us who were lying there on the concrete floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to the rifle butt you mentioned, were you beaten with anything else that you recall?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes. I've told you already about our arrival in the truck. But at the time when they were coming to our cell, I don't know who it was who allowed them to, although there weren't many of them who were beating us, but they would beat us with metal rods, wooden bats. Then I also have scars from knives, metal rods, probably from the baseball bat as well. And you can see all these scars today, you can see them in my face. They would hit me across my teeth, cheekbone, rib cage. They would hit me with the rods in the head, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did the beatings last?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I remember that it would last very long, because many times Ratko would tell me that it -- that the beatings took a long time, because he was not beaten that much. They would beat me most of all. There was one man that they called Budo, Puta, Senad. I don't know whether this was really the name of this particular person. But he would bring in young girls who would -- young women who would laugh. They would set fire to pieces of paper so that they would be able to beat us, because it was in the dark. And my ribs were broken. And this man always pushed me so that I would be lying down on the broken ribs, and then continue beating me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This Budo, did -- do you recall how he was dressed?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Each time differently. He'd show up often, if he was really Budo, because I don't really know the man. But he would have all manner of clothes, like sometimes a camouflage jacket combined with civilian trousers. Sometimes they would enter with weapons, sometimes without the weapons. Whether they would leave them at the reception or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the other people you mentioned who beat you, were they similarly dressed in camouflage, or do you recall if they had civilian clothing on?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Most of them wore camouflage uniforms, although, as I've already said, some wore a combination of military and civilian clothes. And I hope what I'm saying is accurate, because I wouldn't want for a moment to say something that is not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point it would be a good time to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's up to you. If it's convenient for you --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, it is convenient, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll have a 25-minute break. No, I don't think so. We'll have a 25-minute break, starting from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, before we had a break, you were testifying about the beatings that occurred in the prison. You stated that, you testified that your ribs had been injured. Could you tell us how it was, if you recall, when that occurred, and who was beating you at the time? And also if you received any other injuries.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I can explain everything. The first serious injuries I received was in the reception room where my cheekbone was broken as well as my nose by Dzemo Tihic, when he took us out of the cell and into the reception room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did this occur? How long had you been in this particular prison before this incident?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I can't say exactly. I reckon that it was after about half the total time I spent in that prison, maybe 17 or 20. But I'm not sure if this really matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, before we get to your other injuries, could you tell us if the cell, the prison, the cell -- the door to the prison was kept locked during the day? And if it was ever opened, could you tell us when that occurred?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: It happened every day. I'm not sure if the door was locked or not, because the guards were always there. As for the mistreatment and beatings, this occurred on a daily basis. But I pointed out once, I believe, that most of it happened at night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also testified that you would hear a truck stop outside your cell, and that you would hear reference to Chetniks. Could you tell us a little bit more about that in relation to the beatings.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: That's true, I've spoken about that. This truck came from somewhere. It would stop between the court building and the town hall. Then you would hear the sound of the truck and people getting off the truck. They would start yelling and shouting, "Let's go and see the Chetniks." I don't think those were all of them coming. Those who came were only those who were inclined to carry out beatings. There weren't really that many of them, but they always somehow came to the fore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So just for clarification, as soon as you heard the truck stop outside, the beatings would occur shortly thereafter by the people who got off the truck?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: That's true. Most of the times it was those people that beat us, but even before then and after then, we were beaten by people who were purportedly guarding us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also testified that girls would enter the cell. Could you elaborate a little bit more on when this would happen.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes. These young women were brought, most of the times, by the people guarding us. They would set light to small bits of paper, because there was no electricity there, so that they could have enough light to tell our faces. And then they would trample on us and mistreat us. That sort of thing. I'm not sure what else I should tell you about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These girls, were they Muslim or Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Probably Muslim. I find it very difficult to believe that one of us would come there to beat us. Only this lady called Trifunovic, the child who would come in, probably she had been ordered to spit at us and sometimes hit us with a rod. Svetlana. It's not Snezana as I said before. The name is Svetlana. She's a neighbour of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you believe that she was told to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's speculation on his part, clearly. That's going to be pure speculation on this witness's part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's the conclusion that he comes to. Maybe it's the case of explaining why he comes to that conclusion. And I suppose there is a simple answer to that. Why do you come to that conclusion? You say "probably she had been ordered to spit at us and sometimes hit us with a rod." Why do you come to that conclusion? Did you hear anyone instructing her to do this, to spit at you and to hit you with a rod?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was simply enough for me to arrive at that conclusion. I don't believe she would have been doing that of her on accord. She would have no reason to. Why, on earth, would she as a child would walk straight in and start beating us with a rod.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: He was simply he was inferring, that was to make that clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. These are why these are perfectly legitimate questions. Then Obviously you can raise these on cross at any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There shouldn't be invitations to him to speculate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But individuals remain individuals, Mr. Jones. I mean ...

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Eser would like to know approximately the age, the approximate age of this girl? At that time, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, her father's name was Nikola Trifunovic. It's a house I pass very often. I know her well. I don't believe what Your Honour has been talking about, that she would be able to do this of her on free will. I find it perfectly obvious that she must have been ordered to do this by someone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But to answer my question, I only asked you a very simple question: What was her approximate age at the time? That's all I want to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, that. I can only speak to the extent that I knew her, because I had worked abroad a long time, and in Belgrade I never attended any of her birthday parties. But my opinion is that she was about 12 at the time. Perhaps older, perhaps younger. This Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. is my own assessment, as it was at the time, and I shall stick to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did she come from a Muslim family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, from an Orthodox family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, do you know if she was related to Mile Trifunovic, one of the other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes, she was Mile Trifunovic's grandchild.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you were beaten, you stated, I think on more than one occasion, that you lost consciousness. Could you tell us what would happen after you lost consciousness, if you recall.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes. I recall very clearly, they would beat us into unconsciousness. Then they would bring cold water and pour it on us, and then you would barely open your eyes and they would start beating us again, until we were entirely unconscious. I'm speaking on my own behalf, of course. I don't think the others fared any better, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the beatings, you mentioned that your ribs, as well as your -- I think you mentioned also that your teeth were damaged. Was your nose, or any other part of your body, injured as a result of the beatings?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes. The right side of my ribs, two ribs, were fractured. My teeth were entirely damaged. My nose bone was broken three or four times, and my cheekbone also. You can see it. If I press my finger here, it goes up and down. I have countless scars, knife wounds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you had been beaten, and the other prisoners, could you tell us what the physical condition of yourself and the other prisoners were? Was there blood?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's been telling us this, even -- I didn't stop you, but I think he mentioned already that he had injuries to his ribs, broken ribs; he mentioned already that he had a fractured nose; he is mentioned already that for most of the time, he and the other detainees were covered in blood. Why are you repeating the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'll go to the next question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, did there come a time -- I should ask: During the time that you were beaten, were you interrogated by the people who were beating you? Were you questioned during that point?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I don't remember that. They were beating us. Whether they asked us something or not, I really can't say. I must say, I was semi-conscious most of the time. There were times when they came, one of the soldiers probably, if that's what I should call them, a bearded man. He introduced himself as a soldier from Bratunac. He looked at us once from the door. I turned around, to the extent that I could, and he yelled at me, "Listen, Chetnik, even if it were for the whole of Srebrenica, I would never hit you; therefore, you needn't be afraid of me." That was what he said. Unfortunately, the others were much worse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a point in time that you were removed from the cell and taken to another room in this building to be questioned?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes. I remember once - I can't say whether it was more than that - they took me to the reception room where they had the soldiers who watched us. I was taken out of the room and taken to the reception room. I recognised Ismet. He was a person I noticed. Also Tihic, Ahmo Tihic, Ismet Odzic, Ahmo Tihic. I found out who the others were later on, and their names. There were five persons there for sure, up to seven. I'm not sure if this was recorded or not, but it's not important. I saw one man, a bearded man, dark. I can't say that I knew Naser Oric, but when we were returned to the cell after this brief interrogation, the soldiers told me, "Did you see our Delija, Naser?" Some of them said Naser, some of them said the boss. I didn't know the man, though, and I can't say that it was that man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of questions were you asked when you were taken to this room?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I don't remember much. When I came into that room, my left side was totally closed. I was all covered in blood. I do remember that Ahmo or Ismet yelled something along the lines of knowing me well. Why it was like that and why they came, I don't know, but I was not beaten on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that you knew a couple of the individuals in the room you had been taken to. Were they soldiers, as far as you know, or were they civilians?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes, those were soldiers who guarded us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your physical condition during the period of time that you were in this room?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I was in a difficult condition. I had things on my body that were broken, and I was worn down. I told you that I only went out once to relieve myself in the 40 days that I was there. I think that should clarify it sufficiently. I'm not sure what else am I to add.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, were you bleeding at that point?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I don't remember. I know that I was all covered in blood. I think I did say this once. I'm sorry that I didn't bring the shirts along. My wife later washed it, but you can still see traces of blood, stains on the shirt. I said a number of times, "What are you doing that for? Why are you keeping that?" And then she said, "Well, just leave it where it is."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any one of the five men you were in the room with comment on your physical condition?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: No, no one. They would just look at me, and I heard that word being spoken, whether by Ahmo or by Ismet. I don't think I ever caused any harm to those people. And I can even say that I really got along well with them, and I think this can be demonstrated by those of us who are still around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn the identity of anyone else in the room later on, other than Tihic, that you knew from before?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes. I learned later, because he came and went to the hospital and took this man to an exchange, this man named Mandza, whether his first name or last name. I remember Zulfo Tursun. I remember him well. I will tell you more about him later. That's about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you know about Zulfo?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I don't want to be getting ahead of myself. I didn't know him personally, I must make that clear. But I heard that before the war he had murdered a man in a cafe in Srebrenica, one or two persons of his same ethnicity. He was in prison subsequently, and if you want me to talk about him, that's closer to the exchange already. But I can go through the story if you'd like me to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you saw him again, and we'll get -- there came a time that you did see Zulfo again, if you can just answer with a yes or no?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes, I did see him a number of times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the men who were in the room, could you tell us if they were dressed in civilian clothing, including the ones that you know, such as Tihic and Odzic? Were they dressed in civilian clothing or military clothing? And please tell us also the man with the beard.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I really can't say, and I wouldn't like to comment on that. I think I did say that this one man was wearing a camouflage uniform, if I remember correctly, and I believe I do. Some were wearing camouflage uniforms. Whether some were in civilian clothes or not, I didn't exactly take a good look. I was just lying there in front of them. I was like a stone, that's all I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "lying there," do you mean physically lying on the ground in front of them?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly what I mean. If you mean my time in prison, we were all lying, wallowing on that concrete floor, all wet. We were done in. I'm not sure how else I should put it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to when you were in the room, were you lying because you were unable to stand? Or could you tell us what it was that you were lying on the ground?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: We weren't able to stand up, that's certain. We were just simply done in. That's what I'm telling you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to the man with the beard, could you tell us whether you've ever seen him before? And could you describe him to us. In addition to the beard, could you tell us approximately what age he was and whether he was also in a military uniform, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I've said this before, haven't I? This man, he was very dark. He had a beard. A good looking man, rather young. I think I did say that I saw him again somewhere once, but I can't be sure about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn the identity of this man later on?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: He's given a clear answer on that -- on this whole matter. He's said that he returned to his cell, the guard said, "Did you see our Naser," or Delija, our boss or something like that, and he said, "I didn't know the man," and "I can't say that it was that man." That would seem to be the end of it, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, my question is a very specific one, which is: With respect to the man with the beard, did he learn the identity? Not with respect to the comments made by the soldiers. At any point if I learned the identity; if the answer is no, then fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On what basis are you suggesting that he learned the identity?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, he mentioned that he -- he testified that he saw him again, and I would only ask if he later on learned the identity based on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, that dark man that you saw in a room, in the reception room, that you were referred to later by some of the others when they asked you, "That's our Delija, our Naser, did you see him," and you said you didn't know him -- I'll repeat the exact words that you said. "I don't know the name. I can't say that that was the name." What do you know about that? Let's take it bit by bit. At the time had you heard of Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had, but I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you never knew at the time what he looked like.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know. I believe I said that. I never knew that man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So if someone presented you with a person and told you, "This is Naser Oric," you wouldn't have been able to confirm that because you did not know the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not even saying that. I did see him on TV several times later, but I can't say something that's just not true. I didn't know him at the time, because had I known him, he would have been very easy for me to identify then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So -- and who did you see later on on TV several times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, what I'm saying is: Although I saw him on TV several times, I do not want to add something that I didn't actually know at the time. That's what I'm trying to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But are you telling us that on TV, later on, you saw Naser Oric several times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In newspapers too, and on TV. But in person, prior to what we are talking about, I had never known him. And this is why I'm testifying like this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- what I've just told you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- I need to lead you to a very important question now. At the time that all this was happening, you didn't know the person. You had never seen him, you had not met him, so you didn't know what he looked like. And you stand by that position.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I abide by that. When I -- throughout that period of time, in the prison or in the hospital, throughout my captivity, they were saying things like, "This is our Delija, this is Naser, this is the boss." So my idea was always that this must have been the man in the reception room, but that was a later inference that I made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And what inference are you talking about? In other words, later on, when you say on newspapers and on TV the image of what was described as Naser Oric, as I take it from you, was that of any importance for you, looking back to your events in the prison and in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was quite relevant, or seemed quite relevant to me. But again I must say, at the time that I was captured, and throughout my captivity, I'm trying to hold onto that image that I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That you've told us already. Forget about the time that you were captured and what was your position then. Later on, when you saw on TV and on newspapers images of what was described as Naser Oric, did that tell you anything with reference to your detention and to the person that you had seen in the reception -- in the reception room on the occasion that you mentioned? Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I feel, and I'm sure the witness will feel, that you're inviting him to identify someone he saw only later. It seems to me he's being very honest and very adamant in saying he doesn't want to say something about the person --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, please don't stop him, because he also said "inference". He referred to an inference which he drew later from watching TV and from looking at newspapers, and I want to know, what was this inference.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We're also talking about Naser Oric. He never said Oric only. He said, "This is Naser."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, he mentioned Naser Oric, Mr. Jones. He mentioned Naser several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll check in LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When you looked at these newspapers and at the TV, and you said that you drew inferences, what inference did you draw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I arrived at the conclusion later on, when I was looking at the newspapers and watching him on the TV, that that was the person who used to be in the reception room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you left the reception room, did the beatings continue, beatings of yourself and the other prisoners, that is?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: After a while, a silence set in for perhaps an hour or two, and then the situation, as per normal, resumed. There was this person beating us with whatever items came to his hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. There are two questions, one from Judge Eser and then one from me. Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I just have to find the reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. In the meantime, I will ask the question. In this reception room, was Mandza there as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've said so already. Mandza was in this reception room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And did Mandza look similar to the other man, the dark man with the beard? Did they look alike?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. As far as I can remember, Mandza, he did not look like the other man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I would like to bring you back to line 79 -- page 79, line 5. And I go back to the event in the interrogation room or in the reception room. And there you told us: "They would just look at me, and I heard that word being spoken, whether by Ahmo or by Ismet. I don't think I ever caused any harm to those people, and I can even say that I got along well with them. And I think this can be demonstrated by those of us who are still around." Now, my question is: Whom did you mean by saying, "I don't think I ever caused any harm to those people"? Did you speak of yourself? And who are those people? Whom did you mean with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just trying to add what I was previously talking about. I was talking about Ahmo and Ismet were saying. He was the one who told me so, and then I just added. This was my comment, saying that I did not do anything to harm these people. That was just in addition to my previous statement. I don't know if it can be struck off, if need be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: So this was a sort of -- that was not a quotation of what other people said to you, it was your own reflection on this event, so to say; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. This sentence that I repeated here now was an addition of mine. I just wanted to say that I had done nothing wrong to these people, and this can be confirmed by members of their ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I also have an additional question with respect to your meeting in this room. You were asked a series of questions by these men; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes, I do. These people came in, and apart from beating us, they would first address this man Ratko, by asking "Who's Ratko Mladic?" Then he would raise two fingers and then they would beat him, all of them, be it with a rifle, an elbow or a fist or whatever, and then he would fall down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are repeating.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there's a misunderstanding about my question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The room where you were interrogated, where Tihic and Tisanovic and others were present, did they ask you questions in that room, the reception room?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: As I've said, it was more them talking amongst themselves. And then you would have Ratko and Ismet exchanging words. And then after a while, they would just yell, "Take him back to the cell." And then they would take me back there, and after a certain period of time, they would come to beat us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did there come a time that you left the prison cell again, that you were taken out of the prison cell to meet with another individual?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: Yes. After a while - whether it was prior to what we've just been talking about or later on, I can't really grasp - two soldiers took me to the municipal building. I don't know whether it was the first or second floor. They took me to a person who was wearing an olive-drab jacket and a beret on his head. And he started interrogating me, addressing me as a Chetnik, saying that I was killing Muslims. And then I said that I wasn't. And then he asked a couple of other questions that I don't remember, and then he asked me to swear on my children and then I did. But then this soldier came and hit me in the head with a knife. My skin broke and there was blood. The men said, "Take him away, but Chetnik, you will start talking because I'll take you to one of the refrigerator cells." I don't know what he meant by "refrigerator cells," but anyway, after that they returned me to the cell.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have one final question, and I'm looking at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who this man was, the man that you -- that you -- that they took you to see, that the soldiers took you to see?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you who this man was. I just know that he also asked me whether I knew this person by the name of Leskovac, another man by a different name. And he kept asking me about some people, and I kept saying that I didn't know them. After that he hit me with the knife. And I can't remember whether he hit me with the edge or with the blunt side of it, but I can still show you the line, the scar, where he hit me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did he hit you or did the soldier hit you?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic
utterances.text: The soldier did, the one who brought me in in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can end at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Richardson. Incidentally, Mr. Jones, if you look at page 77, line 25, you will see that when he described the man, "I saw one man, a bearded man, dark. I can't say that I knew Naser Oric. But when he returned ..." So he did mention Naser Oric. And that's not the only exception -- the only instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My point was the guards said, "Did you see Naser," they didn't say did you see not Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that's the guards, not him. He knew exactly what person he was being referred to. Anyway, tomorrow, I'm asking you, registrar, please, to consult with the technicians and the interpreters and all the rest of the staff, we need to stop at about between 1:15 and 1:30. The reason is that there is a swearing in of two new ad litem Judges and we need to be present, because it's an official and open ceremony. I wouldn't like to lose as much time as possible. I know that you will not be able to finish tomorrow, and I'm not going to curtail, so you will have all the time you require. So if there is a way to save some time, please try to find it and then let me know tomorrow morning. I don't know if it is possible or not. I know there is a minimum of break time that everyone needs, so I will not curtail that for sure. Perhaps we could have the sittings a little bit longer, in other words, instead of sitting until 10.30, for example, we would sit another quarter of an hour, or another 20 minutes. I don't know, but see what possibilities there are. Yes, again, I mean, for the record, when I said "I wouldn't like to lose as much time as possible," I'm listed as having said "I would like to lose as much time as possible." That certainly isn't the case, so that goes on the record as well. Thank you very much. We will all meet tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
